---
title: "gradient boosting"
---

## intuition

- a fundamentally different way to build a tree ensemble: instead of training many trees independently in parallel and averaging ([random forests](random-forests.qmd)), boosting builds trees **sequentially**, where each new tree corrects the mistakes of everything that came before it
- analogy: one doctor who keeps learning from their own mistakes over time, versus a panel of independent doctors voting

## training, step by step

1. start with a simple initial prediction (e.g. the mean of $y$)
2. look at the current errors (residuals)
3. fit a small tree to predict those residuals
4. add that tree's predictions, scaled by a learning rate, to the running total
5. repeat — each new tree targets whatever error remains after all previous trees

- the final prediction is the initial prediction plus the sum of every tree's scaled correction

## the math: gradient descent in function space

- gradient boosting minimises a loss $l(y,f(x))$ by repeatedly adding a new tree $h_m$ that points in the direction of steepest descent: $f_m(x)=f_{m-1}(x)+\eta\cdot h_m(x)$
- $h_m$ is fit to the negative gradient of the loss — the **pseudo-residuals** — $r_i=-\dfrac{\partial l}{\partial f(x_i)}$
- for squared error loss (regression), these pseudo-residuals are literally the leftover error $y_i-f_{m-1}(x_i)$; for log loss (classification) they're a more complex function of the predicted probabilities, but the same principle holds — see [loss functions](../training-evaluation/loss-functions.qmd)
- this directly parallels [gradient descent](../training-evaluation/gradient-descent.qmd)'s update rule, just in "function space" (adding trees) rather than parameter space (adjusting weights)
- $\eta$, the **learning rate** (or shrinkage), scales how much each new tree's correction counts — a smaller learning rate means each tree contributes less, requiring more trees but usually generalising better

## controlling overfitting

- gradient boosting attacks bias — sequentially driving down error — where random forests attack variance through averaging, see [bias-variance tradeoff](../training-evaluation/bias-variance.qmd); left unchecked, that bias-chasing can itself overfit, so boosting leans on its own regularisation:
  - **learning rate** ($\eta$): smaller values shrink each tree's contribution, trading more trees for better generalisation
  - **number of trees** (`n_estimators`): more trees keep reducing training error, but can eventually overfit without a small enough learning rate
  - **tree depth**: shallow trees (a few levels, sometimes just "stumps") per round, since each tree only needs to capture a small correction
  - **subsampling**: training each round's tree on a random subset of rows and/or columns, similar in spirit to random forests' randomness
- **early stopping** is the standard practical trick: train while watching validation loss after each added tree, and stop once it stops improving — this both prevents overfitting and auto-selects the number of trees, avoiding a separate search over `n_estimators`, see [hyperparameter tuning](../training-evaluation/hyperparameter-tuning.qmd) and [learning curves](../training-evaluation/learning-curves.qmd)

## xgboost vs lightgbm

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| | xgboost | lightgbm |
|---|---|---|
| tree growth | level-wise (breadth-first, balanced trees) | leaf-wise (always splits the leaf with the highest loss reduction) |
| split finding | exact greedy; uses second-order gradients (the hessian) for better convergence | histogram-based approximate splits (binned feature values), plus gradient-based one-side sampling (goss) |
| speed | slower | faster, especially on large datasets |
| overfitting risk | lower by default | higher if not controlled, due to deeper, more irregular trees |

:::

## when to use which

- a single [decision tree](decision-trees.qmd) only when interpretability is the priority and every decision needs to be explainable to a non-technical audience
- [random forests](random-forests.qmd) as a strong, low-effort baseline — hard to badly overfit, minimal tuning required
- gradient boosting (xgboost/lightgbm) when maximum predictive performance matters and there's time to tune it; lightgbm specifically for very large datasets, where histogram binning and leaf-wise growth make it substantially faster

## practical considerations

- boosted trees are more sensitive to their hyperparameters than random forests — learning rate, tree depth, and number of trees interact, so tune them together rather than independently, see [hyperparameter tuning](../training-evaluation/hyperparameter-tuning.qmd)
- use early stopping against a validation set, not the test set — exactly like any other hyperparameter choice, see [train/test splits](../training-evaluation/train-test.qmd)
- as with random forests, feature importance is available but impurity-based importance can be biased toward high-cardinality features
